column1: Ransom Note — given two strings `ransomNote` and `magazine`, return True if ransomNote can be built from letters in magazine. Each magazine letter may be used at most once. Example: ransomNote='aa', magazine='aab' → True.
column2: PATTERN: Frequency counter. | INSIGHT: Count chars in magazine, decrement per ransomNote char; fail if any count goes negative. | STEPS: 1) cnt = Counter(magazine). 2) For c in ransomNote: if cnt[c] == 0 return False; cnt[c] -= 1. 3) Return True. | TIME/SPACE: O(n+m) / O(1) (26 letters). | PITFALL: Comparing lengths is not enough — distribution matters.

column1: Isomorphic Strings — given strings `s` and `t`, return True if they are isomorphic: there is a one-to-one char mapping s→t (no two chars map to the same char; a char may map to itself). Example: s='egg', t='add' → True; s='foo', t='bar' → False.
column2: PATTERN: Bijective hashmap (two dicts). | INSIGHT: Mapping must be one-to-one in BOTH directions, otherwise "ab"→"aa" passes a single map. | STEPS: 1) d1, d2 = {}, {}. 2) For (a,b) in zip(s,t): if a in d1 and d1[a]!=b → False; if b in d2 and d2[b]!=a → False; d1[a]=b, d2[b]=a. 3) Return True. | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(1). | PITFALL: Single hashmap is not enough — need both directions.

column1: Word Pattern — given a `pattern` (chars) and a sentence `s` (space-separated words), return True if s follows the pattern with a bijection between chars and words. Example: pattern='abba', s='dog cat cat dog' → True; pattern='abba', s='dog cat cat fish' → False.
column2: PATTERN: Bijective hashmap on tokens. | INSIGHT: Same as Isomorphic Strings but tokens are space-split words. | STEPS: 1) words = s.split(); if len(words)!=len(pattern) → False. 2) Two dicts char→word and word→char. 3) Walk pairs, enforce bijection. | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(n). | PITFALL: Always check the length-mismatch base case first.

column1: Valid Anagram — given strings `s` and `t`, return True if t is an anagram of s (same multiset of characters). Example: s='anagram', t='nagaram' → True; s='rat', t='car' → False.
column2: PATTERN: Frequency counter (or sort). | INSIGHT: Same length AND same char counts. | STEPS: 1) If len(s)!=len(t) → False. 2) Return Counter(s)==Counter(t). | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(1) for ASCII. | PITFALL: Unicode follow-up → sort or use a dict (not a fixed 26-array).

column1: Group Anagrams — given a list of strings `strs`, group anagrams together and return as a list of lists (any order). Example: ['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat'] → [['eat','tea','ate'],['tan','nat'],['bat']].
column2: PATTERN: Hashmap keyed by canonical form. | INSIGHT: Sorted string OR a 26-tuple of letter counts uniquely identifies an anagram class. | STEPS: 1) groups = defaultdict(list). 2) For w in strs: key = tuple(sorted(w)) (or count tuple). 3) groups[key].append(w). 4) Return list(groups.values()). | TIME/SPACE: O(n·k log k) / O(n·k). | PITFALL: Key must be hashable — use tuple, not list.

column1: Two Sum — given an integer array `nums` and integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add to target. Exactly one solution; cannot use the same element twice. Example: nums=[2,7,11,15], target=9 → [0,1].
column2: PATTERN: Complement hashmap. | INSIGHT: For each num, the partner we need is target-num; record indices as we go. | STEPS: 1) seen = {}. 2) For i,n in enumerate(nums): if target-n in seen → return [seen[target-n], i]; seen[n]=i. | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(n). | PITFALL: Insert AFTER the check so an element doesn't pair with itself.

column1: Happy Number — given integer `n`, return True if it is "happy": repeatedly replacing n with the sum of squares of its digits eventually reaches 1 (otherwise it cycles forever). Example: n=19 → True (19 → 1+81=82 → 68 → 100 → 1).
column2: PATTERN: Cycle detection on a functional sequence. | INSIGHT: Sequence either hits 1 or enters a cycle — detect cycle with a set (or Floyd's two-pointer for O(1) space). | STEPS: 1) seen = set(). 2) While n!=1 and n not in seen: seen.add(n); n = sum(int(d)**2 for d in str(n)). 3) Return n==1. | TIME/SPACE: O(log n) / O(log n). | PITFALL: Floyd's tortoise/hare gives O(1) space if asked.

column1: Contains Duplicate II — given an integer array `nums` and integer `k`, return True if there exist distinct indices i,j with nums[i]==nums[j] AND |i-j| ≤ k. Example: nums=[1,2,3,1], k=3 → True; nums=[1,2,3,1,2,3], k=2 → False.
column2: PATTERN: Hashmap of last-seen index (sliding window). | INSIGHT: Only the most recent index of each value matters. | STEPS: 1) last = {}. 2) For i,n in enumerate(nums): if n in last and i-last[n]<=k → True; last[n]=i. 3) Return False. | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(min(n,k)). | PITFALL: Always overwrite last[n] — old indices are useless.

column1: Longest Consecutive Sequence — given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (in any positions). Must run in O(n). Example: nums=[100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (the run 1,2,3,4).
column2: PATTERN: Hashset + only-start-from-sequence-start. | INSIGHT: Only count from n where n-1 is NOT in the set; this guarantees each element is visited at most twice → O(n). | STEPS: 1) s = set(nums). 2) For n in s: if n-1 not in s: walk n+1, n+2... while in s, track length. 3) Return max length. | TIME/SPACE: O(n) / O(n). | PITFALL: Without the n-1 guard you re-walk sequences and degrade to O(n²).
